heading: 2. Problem analysis

heading: 3.Literature Review
note: 1 block, 1 group, 328 words — the whole review is a single measured paragraph because the PDF sets it as one justified block spanning pp. 4-5. Eight references are walked in citation order with the use made of each stated: [1] Wang/Hu international-equity definition, [6] Li enterprise organisational structure, [2] Ge/Liu RAP fairness indicators and selection criteria, [3] Hu Angang national-power indicator set, [4] Liu Huihong cooperative-competition game, [5] Liu Zhiyun feasibility of international distributive justice, [7] Xue Fenghua Shapley revenue allocation, [8] Zeng Zhi'e space ethics. It closes on the gap ('However, there are few studies on asteroid mining') and then the block's tail carries the '4. Basic assumption' heading. Zero numbers, zero formulas: the chapter is context, not argument. Note that the reference numbering here skips [6] ahead of [2]-[5] but the bibliography on p. 25 is in numeric order.

heading: 4. Basic assumption
note: 3 blocks, 3 groups, three '⚫ It is assumed that' bullets, each one printed line split across the block boundary with its continuation: (1) 'the countries with asteroid mining capabilities remain fixed for a short period of time'; (2) 'in cooperation, there is stable cooperation between countries and no country intentionally interferes with cooperation'; (3) 'countries initially operate independently of each other when mining asteroids'. No justification sentence is attached to any of the three — the chapter states scope restrictions and moves on, which is why every job is limit rather than derive. Block 47's tail carries '5. Glossary & Symbols Glossary:'. Assumption 3 is the load-bearing one for chapter 7 (the n-country oligopoly is built on independent initial operation).

heading: 6.Our work (Figure 2 flow chart) / 6.1 Expansion of Theil index
note: 11 blocks, 9 groups. 61 is the '6.Our work Figure 2 Full Text Flow Chart' heading plus caption, read as a figure block because the diagram itself carries no text. 62 is the '6. heading: 6.2 Measurement of comprehensive national power
note: 14 blocks, 9 groups. 72 is the '6.2' heading, grouped with 73 ('In a complex world, measuring the comprehensive power of a country is a very arduous and abstract task ... this paper adopts a factor analysis strategy') which also carries the '◆ Step1: Selection of variables' marker. 74-75 select eight plus variables and open Table 2 ('GDP, Territory Area, Official Expenses, Military production per capita, Technology level, telephone lines, population, International Trade, health, Internet, Population, education'), 76 is the table's data-source line '(Data source:world Bank,Knoema)' printed after the rows. 77-78 print the normalisation eq (4) plus 'where S is the sample standard deviation' and the '◆ Step2: Calculation of the correlation coefficient matrix R' marker. 79-80 diagonalise R and dismiss the residual ('A is a number so small as to be negligible'). 81-82 are the only computation with a stated threshold: 'the sum of the contributions of the first three factors has exceeded 80%', therefore m = 3. 83 prints the composite-score eq (5). 84 is Table 3 'Table of countries' composite power scores (normalized)' in one block: United States 0.953, China 0.860, India 0.712, Mexico 0.693, Dominican Rep 0.483, Sudan 0.452, Chad 0.256, Haiti 0.249 — eight countries, exactly the sample; the table header prints a stray 'year' column label but no years, and no loadings or factor scores are printed anywhere, so 0.953 cannot be reproduced from the text. 85 promises more ('In order to make the sample more general, not all countries that are major players in the international community are chosen as the sample in this paper, The following chart shows the spread of scores') but no figure or caption follows, so the promised score-spread chart is missing from the paper.

heading: 6.3 Test of the Equity Measurement Model (6.3.1 historical, 6.3.2 regional)
note: 15 blocks, 9 groups. 86-87 state the test design and cite the properties: 'this criterion ... needs to satisfy the endogenous principle of inequity, on the one hand, and the historical and geographical test, on the other. According to the citation [2], the Theil index satisfies the scale-invariance, transfer principle, and decomposability principle, having good applicability.' 88-89 justify the historical window ('we can compress the modern decades into an interval of relatively constant conditions on the time axis') — an honest statement that the index is only compared within an era. 90-91 are the grading step that everything later depends on: 'we can classify countries into four categories' A-D, but the cut points are never printed. 92 is the 'Figure 5 Theil index change curve' caption. 93 reads it: A and B fall (fairer), D is flat, C rises (less fair), and 'in the longitudinal comparison ... the B-rank curved Theil index is higher than A, while A is h...'. 94-95 open 6.3.2 ('Regional validation inherits the classification of countries in historical validation'), 96-97 plot pairwise combinations with the 'Figure 6 Theil index chart for different combinations' caption, and 98-100 read the one fact used: the A-grade/D-grade combination 'produces a large Theil index, indicating a very uneven fairness of this combination and in line with the objective laws of reality'. Every check here is qualitative — no p-value, no residual, no hold-out; the only quantitative anchor in the whole test is the 80% variance threshold back in 6.2.

heading: 6.3.3 Sensitivity test of selection index
note: 4 blocks, 3 groups. 101 is the heading, grouped with 102 which states the perturbation: 'we observe the change in the Thiel index by varying all indicators for C-rank countries up and down by 5% at the same time, using 2017 as an example'. Only one grade (C) and one year (2017) are perturbed, so this is a single-point check, not a sweep over the 2017-2019 window the rest of the paper plots. 103 is the 'Figure 7 Graph of index change with rate of change' caption; 104 reads it as 'the Theil index decreases significantly as the rate of change increases, signifying that the Theil index is sensitive to changes in the indicators, which also indicates that fairness is more pronounced with changes in the indicators' — the last clause is a non-sequitur: a falling index means less measured inequality, not that fairness improves because indicators move. The 5% is the only number in the chapter; no elasticity or rank-stability table is given.

heading: 6.3.4 Fairness, justice and our world (Gini cross-check)
note: 4 blocks, 3 groups. 105 is the '6.3.4' heading grouped with 106, which explains why a second index is used at all: 'The Gini coefficient, unlike the Theil index, is not decomposable, but can be used to measure the income gap between residents of a country or region.' 107 is the plot plus its caption ('Using matlab, we obtain a plot of the overall Gini coefficient over time for the whole world: Figure 8 World Overall Gini Coefficient Chart') — machine and tooling are named, the data source is not. 108 reads the result: 'the overall Gini coefficient is stable between 0.4 and 0.44, the relative fluctuation trend is not strong, the overall fairness of the world does not change abruptly, but the overall but the fairness of the gap is large' (duplicated 'the overall but' is in the source). The cross-check is directional only: the paper's own Theil series must be read as roughly flat to agree with 0.40-0.44, which fights the 'C grade rises' finding of 6.3.1 unless C is a small share of the population — the paper never reconciles the two.

heading: 7. Problem II / 7.1 Oligarchic model - from competition to cooperation
note: 13 blocks, 7 groups. The chapter title is split over two heading blocks (109 '7. Problem II The Development of an Oligarchic Model', 110 'and the Impact on World Equity') and the two sub-headings 111 '7.1 Oligarchic model - from competition to cooperation' and 112 '7.1.1 Cooperative competition model for oligopolistic countries' follow immediately, so the four heading blocks form one route group. 113-114 give the premise and the source: 'not all countries have the conditions and ability to go to asteroid mining ... there will be n powerful, resource-rich "oligopoly" countries to create a monopoly' then 'Combining the references [4], we can model the n-oligopoly competitive game using the country analogy to a firm'. 115 opens the notation ('Assume that there are n countries in the world that have the ability to travel extraterrestrial for mining. order:') and the symbols it introduces are lost — the defining display is not in the text layer. 116-117 carry the solution sentence and eq (6) with the '7.1.2 International Cooperative Competitive Equilibrium and International Nash Equilibrium' heading in 117's tail. 118-119 give the Nash equilibrium and the full-cooperation case ('In contrast, when fully cooperative Thus exists:'). 120 is the comparison group: cooperative-competition equilibrium beats both full competition and full cooperation ('more realistic compared to the full cooperation model (e.g. two countries with different languages and scripts)'). 121 is the hand-off: 'the first countries to participate in interstellar mineral extraction will move from competition to cooperation based on their own interests. Is this the end?' — the question is answered by the next chapter. No numbers: the model is solved symbolically and nothing is calibrated or simulated here.

heading: 7.2 Further fragmentation of the Developing and the Developed
note: 6 blocks, 5 groups. 122 is the heading and 123 the rhetorical turn ('It looks like the countries that were able to do interstellar mining achieved their goal of establishing a relatively equitable distribution system, but what about the rest of them?'), grouped together. 124 states the mechanism that the second half of the paper runs on: 'if there is only cooperation and monopoly among the oligopolies, the global inequity will be greatly aggravated. Figure 9 Different Voices'. 125 is the first counterfactual, and its assumptions are coarse: 'Assume in 2005 discovered a human named "Lucky" alien mineral ... the exploitation of the country's GDP will rise by 15%', with the mining sample cut to seven space-launching countries (USA, Russia, Japan, UK, France, China, India) instead of the eight-country factor sample, while the factor scores are still taken 'in combination with the previous method'. 126 is the 'Figure 10 Change in Theil's index before and after the emergence of Lucky' caption; 127 reads three pairwise curves ('yes.no', 'yes.yes', 'no.no') and concludes the mining/non-mining gap spikes after 2005. The 15% is arbitrary and no sensitivity is run on it — the single largest unexamined number in chapter 7.

heading: 7.3 Asteroid Mining Vision
note: 45 blocks, 11 groups — the longest chapter in the paper and entirely prescriptive. 128 sets the frame ('With reference[5] to the principles and examples of previous international cooperation, this paper will present a vision for the development of asteroid mineral resources based on the following principles'). Three ➢ principles follow, each split one printed line per block: freedom of choice in distribution (129-133), developed-country assistance and compensation to developing countries across institutions, management, human resources, research, information and patent transfer (134-140), and a UN-run redistribution system with crisis relief (141-146). 147-150 then switch from principle to mechanism: 'If extraterrestrial deposits exist as a common asset of mankind, then every independent country is entitled to a "planetary area" of its own ... our team offers three different ways out for the remaining countries'. The three ✓ ways out are joint mining for countries with capital but no launch capability (151-153), UN-held 'planetary area' until a country can mine independently (154-157), and tender/auction of the area for countries in extreme poverty or perennial war (158-160). 161 is the institutional design group: the European Coal and Steel Community analogy, the 'Figure 11 each takes what he needs' caption inside the same block, and the pivot ('international cooperation is needed to achieve equity, so the following analysis focuses on joint development') that launches the policy bullets 162-172 (contract downstream industry to less-developed countries, cap capital expansion and private monopoly, break trade barriers, crack down on transnational speculation). No quantity, no cost, no schedule: everything here is a normative hand-off, and the only numbers anywhere in the chapter are the figure numbers.

heading: 7.4 The impact of asteroid mineral extraction on world equity
note: 15 blocks, 8 groups. 173 is the 7.4 heading with 174, which names the frame and its deviation: 'we divide the country into n non-adversarial subjects ... Consistent with the Shapley model. However, unlike the traditional Shapley model, the model in this paper focuses on the effects of distribution on fairness.' 175 carries the '7.4.1 simulation mining model of Lucky2' heading and defines the second counterfactual — but circularly: 'the GDP of the country where Lucky2 is mined will rise corresponding to the value of Lucky2', so Lucky2 has no magnitude of its own and the 15% of Lucky is never formally replaced. 176-182 are seven symbol glosses orphaned from their displays ('represents no revenue if mining is not performed', 'represents the characteristic function of the sharply value', 'represents the role of lucky2 to make the rise in GDP occur', 'is the formula previously obtained using factor analysis'), i.e. the equations themselves are not in the text layer and the definitions cannot be checked. 183 is the Monte Carlo result with the paper's only Shapley numbers: 'the value of the 30th row and the 30th column is the largest, and the corresponding Shapley Value after equal scaling is 0.6437 and 0.5982', read as 'the gain is maximized when the countries that have the ability to mine have a slightly higher contribution ... than the countries that do not'. 0.6437/0.5982 sum to 1.2419, so the 'equal scaling' is not to unity and the two numbers cannot be read as shares. 184 allocates by Shapley to get WPI and the Theil plot; 185-186 are the 'Figure 13 Post-Collaboration Theil Index Chart' and 'Figure 14 Changes in the global Theil coefficient after mining' captions, each its own group; 187 reads both ('Theil index under each combination has decreased ... especially for the countries that have the ability to extract versus those that do not'). The chapter therefore runs on a heat map whose axes are country counts, not the 15% GDP shock of 7.2, and never says how the two simulations relate.

heading: 7.5 Analysis of results and conclusions
note: 3 blocks, 2 groups. 188 is the '7.5' heading grouped with 189, the section summary, which restates the whole chapter chain in one paragraph: pioneers cooperate for profit, monopoly spikes the Theil index, so 'a reasonable international cooperation system and a fair international distribution system must be established. With the distribution according to labor as the main body, combined with the distribution according to the means of production ...'. 190 closes the chapter on a directive ('Countries that are capable of independent mining should respond positively to international cooperation ... money for money, power for power') and is the chapter's close marker. The summary inherits the chapter's weakest link uncorrected: the 'spike in Theil index' comes from Lucky's 15% shock, while the cooperation result comes from a Shapley model that never uses that shock.

heading: 8. Problem III / 8.1 Path analysis of the impact of mineral extraction on the country
note: 10 blocks, 6 groups. 191 is the section heading ('8. Problem III Development characteristics of the simulation mining model') grouped with 192, the plan: 'This section will first discuss the "actual impact" ... using a path analysis ... followed by an analysis of changes in world equity from three perspectives: the technology explosion, interest groups, and the resource curse.' 193-195 carry the '8.1' and '◆ Step1' markers and select the path variables with a pointer backwards ('draw the flux diagram (See previous table2 for original variables)') — so the path model's variable set is Table 2's twelve indicators, unchanged. 196 introduces the third counterfactual: 'the introduction of W as a new variable, meaning the profit gained by the country after participating in the mineral development ... here also introduced a magical mineral Lucky3, mining in the country will be an overall increase of 0.05 in the rating of indicators (the score has been normalized)'. 197-198 are one read-figure group because 197 only announces the plot ('assuming that Lucky3 is mined in the sample countries mentioned in the previous section, the pathways are plotted') and 198 is the caption 'Figure 15 Schematic diagram of through-hole analysis' — 'through-hole' is the literal translation of 通径 (path), and the diagram is the path model. 199 opens Step2 with a parenthetical ('Each of the c in the diagram interacts with each other'), 200 gives the estimator ('where r is the simple correlation coefficient and p is the flux diameter') and closes on '◆ Step3: Analysis of results'. heading: 8.1 Step3 Analysis of results (path coefficients)
note: 5 blocks, 2 groups. 201-204 are one measured group, a single answer split one printed line per block: the path coefficients single out GDP, international trade and per capita income, 'which further affects global equity', and the reading is a plausibility claim rather than a test ('The result is logical and reflects the fact that the real sector influences global equity primarily by affecting a range of economic indicators.'). The three coefficients quoted in the abstract (0.45, 0.38, 0.29) are not printed anywhere in the body — the body names the three variables and no magnitude, so the abstract's numbers cannot be traced. 205 opens 8.2 and its tail carries the '8.2.1 Technological Explosion and the Rise of Nations' heading; job route because it only frames what follows.

heading: 8.2.1 Technological Explosion and the Rise of Nations
note: 13 blocks, 5 groups. 206-209 set the hypothesis in four split lines ('if there are certain countries involved in asteroid mining that have seized the opportunity of the times and achieved rapid growth in their own productivity, explore the impact on international equity'). 210-215 build the counterfactual, and the substitution is worth recording: Brazil is chosen as 'with a relatively average population and development level', then 'the value of manufactured goods in France grows from 2 billion to nearly 15 billion francs between 1870 and 1897 in the Second Industrial Revolution, assuming that its economy grows linearly at a very fast rate, and assuming that Brazil's GDP grows linearly at the same rate as France in the Second Industrial Revolution between 2005 and 2015'. A French 1870-1897 growth rate is transplanted onto Brazil 2005-2015 as a stand-in for a productivity explosion — the rate itself is never computed from the 2bn->15bn span (that would be about 7.5x over 27 years, ~7.6% a year). 216 is the 'Figure 16 Emerging Countries Rising Equity Curve' caption; 217 reads it ('The Theil index decreases and produces a rebound after a period of time. So we conclude that the globe becomes more equitable over time') — a rebound inside the window is acknowledged and then dropped from the conclusion. 218 supplies the caveat the reading lacked ('Although few countries, in reality, have linear economic growth, once a country's strength continues to grow rapidly, a new "unipolarity" is formed, which threatens global equity.') and glues the '8.2.2 Resource Curse' heading to its tail.

heading: 8.2.2 Resource Curse / 8.2.3 Generated interest groups
note: 7 blocks, 6 groups. 219 is the background sentence with no number attached ('Since the 1980s, more and more resource-rich countries have fallen into the growth trap, the resource curse'), kept as context. 220 states the scenario and its grade mapping — 'if countries that exploit space (the previous category B countries) are overly dependent on space-rich mineral resources causing their economies to stagnate (assuming they remain unchanged), while other countries' economies grow as usual according to historical data, calculate the change in global equity from 2010' — but the equation of 'countries that exploit space' with 'the previous category B countries' is asserted, not shown: the space-capable list in 7.2 was USA/Russia/Japan/UK/France/China/India, and the A-D grades were never printed. 221 is the reading and it contradicts itself inside one paragraph: 'the trend of Theil index decreasing and then increasing after the introduction of the resource trap is more obvious' followed by 'the world fairness in general shows a trend of increasing and then decreasing'. 222 is the mechanism conjecture (path dependence, single economic structure, wars over resources) and is the chapter's causal payoff. 223-224 group the '8.2.3' heading with the OPEC analogy: 'just as oil resources have given rise to the OPEC organization ... the model will degenerate back to the n-oligarchy game model, which will lead to a spike in th(e)...' — this is the one place that closes the loop with chapter 7. 225 is a one-sentence corollary ('In the process of implementing mining, opposing monopoly is also a very important issue.') and hands to chapter 9.

heading: 9. UN Charter for Asteroid Development
note: 40 blocks, 12 groups. The chapter is structured as three quoted UN Charter preamble clauses, each followed by policies derived from it. 226-227 open with the frame ('The United Nations should be guided by the universal values enshrined in the UN Charter in formulating policies ... based on the preamble of the UN Charter'). Quote 1: 'WE THE PEOPLES OF THE UNITED NATIONS DETERMINED / to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war' (228-230, context) followed by mining bills on UN approval of equipment, a space-weapons ban, and the right to suspend violating countries (231-236). Quote 2: 'to reaffirm faith in fundamental human rights' (237-238) followed by people-first safety (239-241), small-country participation (242-244, citing [8]) and women's employment protection (245-247). Quote 3: 'to establish conditions under which justice and respect for the obligations arising from treaties ... can be maintained' (248) followed by international-law authority, a mediation committee and legal aid for weaker states (249-253). 254-258 is a mixed group: a sustainability policy over 'population, natural resources, economic, social and political conditions', then 'we select population density, and gain the effect of the country's population density on policies. As shown in figure 10, you can see the population policy follows, and the influence of economic policy is the minimum' — the pointer is wrong (Figure 10 is the Lucky Theil chart on p. 14, not a policy figure), and the claim is the only quantitative statement in the chapter. 258's tail carries '⚫ to promote social progress and better standards of life in larger freedom', so quote 4 and its policies (intergenerational equity and extraction limits 259-261, price regulation; smuggling monitoring and civilian use of new technology 262-265) run to the chapter end. Every group here is a hand-off: no cost, no instrument, no enforcement analysis, and no linkage back to the Theil index.

heading: 10. Evaluation and Spread of the Model
note: 18 blocks, 7 groups. 266 is the '10. Evaluation and Spread of the Model' heading with 267 ('10.1 Evaluation of the Model 10.1.1 Strengths'). The strengths are one group per problem: Problem 1 (268-269, factor analysis compresses the indicator set and 'the innovative way of combining factor scores with the Theil index makes the results more objective and convincing'); Problem 2 (270-275, six split lines: cooperative games plus multi-objective programming plus Monte Carlo, the derive-then-distribute-then-simulate order, 'It is very clever to assume that the historical data is unknown and use the real historical data as the object of comparison'); Problem 3 (276-280, path analysis with a new element and pre-specified Monte Carlo factors). 280's tail carries '10.1.2 Weaknesses', and 281 is the limitation paragraph: the model 'cannot predict all the development of asteroid mining, which makes the model have certain time limit and limitation' and 'Monte Carlo simulation is used several times in this paper for solving, which makes the generality of the results weak' — the second is the honest one and it undercuts every simulated result in chapters 7-8. 282 opens '10.2 The Extension of Models' (the cooperative game transfers to resource allocation 'within countries, companies') and 283 continues it into future scenario simulation while carrying the 'Appendix Stata code:(Theil index)' heading in its tail, so the appendix and the reference list (284-288) are inside this block's boundary but are not coded chapters.
